Chileab
KIL-ee-ab
n. (the second son of David, borne by Abigail at Hebron; called Daniel in 1 Chronicles)
Hebrew Kil'ab, probably like his father, or restraint of the father; the Authorized Version margin at 2 Samuel 3:3 gives “or, Daniel,” the name under which 1 Chronicles 3:1 records him.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

Chileab was David's second son, born at Hebron: “And his second, Chileab, of Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite; and the third, Absalom the son of Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur” (2 Samuel 3:3). The Chronicler gives the same man another name: “Now these were the sons of David, which were born unto him in Hebron; the firstborn Amnon, of Ahinoam the Jezreelitess; the second Daniel, of Abigail the Carmelitess” (1 Chronicles 3:1), and the Authorized Version margin at 2 Samuel notes the equivalence. He is not Daniel the prophet; he is David's son by the woman who had been Nabal's wife. Nothing else is recorded of him — no exploit, no sin, no death — and that silence is itself worth something. His elder brother Amnon raped his sister; his younger brother Absalom murdered Amnon and then rebelled against his father. Chileab is the one son of Hebron who never appears again. The house was born in a season of attrition: “Now there was long war between the house of Saul and the house of David: but David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker” (2 Samuel 3:1), and the sons listed in those verses — by several different mothers — are the fruit of a polygamy that would tear the household apart.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Chileab is a biblical proper name and has no entry in Webster's dictionary of the English language.

expand to see more

Chileab is the name of the second son of David; Webster's 1828 dictionary treats common English words and does not define it.

It occurs once in the Authorized Version, at 2 Samuel 3:3.

The Hebrew is probably like his father, or restraint of the father.

The Authorized Version margin gives “or, Daniel,” the name used at 1 Chronicles 3:1.

He is not Daniel the prophet; his mother was Abigail, Nabal's widow.

Modern Corruption

David's many wives are read as a cultural detail, where 2 Samuel lists the sons of several mothers and then narrates the household destroying itself.

expand to see more

The list of sons born at Hebron is a list of different mothers, and the chapters that follow are rape, fratricide and rebellion inside that one household. Scripture does not editorialise; it narrates, and the narration is the judgment. The dictionary holds marriage as one man and one woman, which is the creational ordinance the Lord Himself appeals to, and it reads the collapse of David's family as the Bible's own commentary on departing from it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a son of whom nothing bad is recorded is a mercy in a chapter of disasters, and that one man may be given two names in Scripture without the record being in error.
